A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the transition delay is due to the suppression of the secondary instability by the upstream deformation, but the delay is not as large as expected from the secondary-instability theory, which is attributed to the fact that the flow deformation is not a pure crossflow-vortex mode but a combination of a crossflow-vorticity mode and a streamwise-vorticity mode.

the secondary instability of saturated crossflow vortex structures is a key factor in the laminar breakdown of a three-dimensional boundary-layer flow, and that the spanwise vortex structure of saturated crossflow-vortex packets is a decisive factor in the onset of the secondary instability.

The main takeaway from our work is that

crossflow vortex-induced transition is a complex phenomenon, and the secondary instability of saturated crossflow vortex modes is convective, with the convective nature being more pronounced the larger the spanwise wavelength of the saturated vortices.
the transition control strategy is based on a subtle balance between the nonlinear vortex modes and the base flow, which can be achieved by a proper choice of the vortex mode.

a transition delay by upstream flow deformation is only possible for a favourable pressure gradient, and the delay is more effective if the flow is deformed by a packet of crossflow-vortices rather than by single crossflow vortex modes.
